idiom_name: interface value (implicit satisfaction) as the envelope
implementation_notes: Go's interface value already is an envelope: a variable of interface type stores any value whose method set satisfies the interface, with no implements clause anywhere, and calling a method on it dispatches through the runtime-built method table. The letter is any value with the right methods - io.Writer's single Write method is the canonical minimal letter - and swapping the implementation is an ordinary assignment to that variable. What replaces the classic structure is therefore the interface type itself plus, when a named API is wanted, a small struct holding it; the copy-semantics half of the C++ idiom has no Go analogue, because Go has no copy constructors and no clone protocol.
pitfalls: A nil interface value and an interface value holding a nil pointer behave differently: calling a method on the first panics, on the second it runs and may dereference nil - checking err != nil style guards is not enough.
Assigning a value type with methods on pointer receivers does not satisfy the interface (the method set of T lacks them); pass &T instead.

Boxing a large struct into an interface copies it to the heap (only word-sized values avoid the allocation), so an envelope field holding a big letter by value silently allocates on every assignment - store a pointer.
